GETTING STARTED

The Beginner's Starter Kit: What You Actually Need (And What You Don't)

FROM THE ACADEMY

Every beginner does the same thing when they get serious about detailing: they open a forum, a YouTube comment section, or a Facebook group, and they start buying. A soap here, a coating there, three different microfiber towel brands because someone swore one was better. Within a month they've got forty bottles on a shelf and no real sense of what any of them are actually for.

That's not a starter kit. That's a distraction with a barcode.

Why more products makes you worse, not better

When you own forty products, you spend more mental energy deciding what to use than actually using it well. You never get repetitions with any single product, so you never build real feel for how it behaves — how much pressure it needs, how long it dwells, what it looks like when it's working versus when it's not. Skill comes from repetition. Repetition requires narrowing down, not stacking up.

The fastest way to get good is to get boring: pick a small kit and use it on every job until it's second nature.

What actually belongs in a beginner's kit

WHEEL, TIRE & BUG CLEANER

Superior Products — Dark Fury

Non-acid wheel and tire cleaner that also happens to be one of the best bug removers on paint I've used — spray it on, let it dwell, rinse. One bottle, does double duty.

Get Dark Fury →
RINSELESS WASH CONCENTRATE

UNDRDOG — Rinseless Wash Concentrate

This is the one that replaces half your shelf. Wash the car, use it as a clay lube, wipe down interior plastics, clean the windows — basically everything except wheels and tires — all from one bottle, diluted at an incredible rate. If you only add one "extra" to the kit, make it this.

Get the Rinseless Concentrate →
MICROFIBER TOWELS

A couple of quality towels

A dedicated drying towel is non-negotiable — it's the difference between a streak-free finish and water spots baked into the paint. Pair it with one more towel for wax or sealant application. Not ten different kinds. Two, used correctly.

QUICK DETAILER / SEALANT

UNDRDOG — Quick Detailer

The one product worth not cheaping out on — hands down, no contest. Learn its cure time, its look, how it lays down. Don't rotate between five "just to see."

Get the Quick Detailer →
CLAY BAR

3D — Clay Bar

This is the one that actually separates a detail from a wash. A car can look clean and still be covered in bonded contaminants you can't see — clay is what pulls that off and gives you a truly smooth, prepped surface. Pair it with a dedicated lubricant so it glides instead of dragging.

Get the Clay Bar →
ALL-PURPOSE CLEANER

3D — Super Citrus APC

For the stuff Rinseless can't touch — heavy soiling, grease, fabric stains, floor mats that have seen better days. A citrus-based APC cuts through grime without eating up plastics or fading colors, and it's dilutable enough to stretch a long way.

Get the Citrus APC →

The gear that rounds it out

None of this needs a specific brand — just don't skip it. This is the equipment that makes the products above actually work the way they're supposed to.

WASH SPONGE

A dedicated rinseless wash sponge

This one's actually built specifically for rinseless washing — stays dedicated to paint contact only, never used on wheels, tires, or anything gritty. That's how swirls happen.

Round it out with a few spray bottles for diluting the Rinseless and Citrus APC at different strengths, a bucket or two for rinsing towels between passes, and a hose for the one spot where rinseless doesn't apply — wheels, tires, and heavy brake dust need an actual rinse.

That's it. That's the list. Everything else is something you add later, once you've actually mastered what's already in your hands — not because a forum told you to buy it.

The real cost of the forty-bottle shelf

It's not just the money, though that adds up fast. It's the time. Every hour spent comparing products online is an hour not spent on a car, not building the actual skill that pays your bills. Beginners who narrow down early get good faster — not because they're more talented, but because they're not splitting their attention forty ways.

Start small. Get good at small. Expand once small stops being a challenge.
